unit.title: The Silk Road: Medieval Trade Networks

lesson.title: More Than Goods: Ideas on the Silk Road
lesson.subject: social-studies

contentBlocks.text: Yesterday you learned what the Silk Road was. Today: what actually traveled along it!

Real goods traveled the Silk Road: silk from China, spices from South Asia, and many other valuable items. But goods weren't the only thing exchanged — religions, technologies like paper-making, and even diseases spread along these same routes, connecting distant cultures in both directions. Name one good and one non-material thing (an idea, technology, or religion) that spread along the Silk Road.
You just learned the Silk Road exchanged far more than goods! Tomorrow we'll connect this to Punjab's own trade position.

objectives: Name real goods that traveled the Silk Road (silk, spices)
Understand that ideas, technologies, and religions also spread along these routes
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review yesterday's Silk Road network lesson.
2. Introduce goods and non-material exchange (ideas, technology, religion).
3. Have the child name one of each.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's Punjab-connection lesson.
differentiationTips: Struggling: focus on just one clear goods example (silk) and one clear idea example (a religion spreading to a new region)
Ready for more: ask the child why exchanging ideas and technology might have mattered even more than exchanging goods, in the long run
This lesson deliberately broadens 'trade' beyond just goods, a genuine historical-thinking step up
teacherGuide.answerKey: This is a recall activity — check that the child names a real good (silk, spices, paper) and a real non-material exchange (a religion, paper-making technology, or another verifiable idea).
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses the course's 'medieval through early modern world' description, deepening the Silk Road's real historical significance beyond simple trade goods.
